title: Unit 11 Quiz · Final Synthesis: Young Geographer-Citizen Exhibition
description: 10 questions about Unit 11. Read each question carefully. Pick the best answer. One question asks you to pick all the answers that are true.

questions.lesson: 3.11.01 Review: See the Place, Hear the Voices, Follow the Story
questions.text: Your exhibit has four parts. What are they?
options: Every fact you know about the place.
A map, a source, a community connection, and a virtue.
A title, a poem, a song, and a game.
One big picture with no words.
questions.why: A strong exhibit has four parts: a map, a source, a community connection, and a virtue. In 3.11_02 each part became one slide, after a Welcome slide.

questions.text: Which is the strongest label for a map slide?
options: "Map."
"This is a very nice map."
"This map shows the Northeast, where many big cities and old harbors are."
A long list of every fact about the Northeast, with big, fancy words.
questions.why: A strong label names the place and says why it matters, in a few clear words a visitor can read fast.

questions.text: True or false: More words always make a slide better.
options: True
False
questions.why: False. Courtesy for a visitor means short, clear words and a real picture. Too many words make a visitor walk away.

questions.lesson: 3.11.03 Present the Evidence: Map, Source, and Virtue
questions.text: A walk-through has five steps. What is the LAST step?
options: Greet the visitor.
Read every word on the slide, very fast.
Tell the visitor every fact you know.
Name the virtue, then ask: "Do you have any questions?"
questions.why: The five steps are: greet, show the map, explain the source, point to the community, and end with the virtue and an invitation to ask a question.

questions.lesson: 3.11.03 Present the Evidence: Map, Source, and Virtue
questions.text: A visitor asks you a question, and you don't know the answer. What does an honest guide say?
options: "Good question. I'm not sure, but here is what I do know."
Make up an answer that sounds smart.
Pretend you didn't hear the question.
"I know everything about this place."
questions.why: An honest guide says "I'm not sure" and then shares what they really know. Making things up is not honest.

questions.lesson: 3.11.03 Present the Evidence: Map, Source, and Virtue
questions.text: A real photo shows a farmer and his sons walking through a dust storm in 1936. Which sentence is honest?
options: "This photo proves the Great Plains is always dusty."
"This photo proves every farm had a dust storm."
"This photo shows a farmer and his sons walking through a dust storm in 1936."
"This is the best photo anyone ever took."
questions.why: A source shows some things, not everything. An honest guide says what the photo shows and does not stretch it.

questions.text: Pick ALL the habits of a young geographer-citizen.
options: See the world carefully.
Use evidence honestly.
Always have the loudest opinion in the room.
Serve the common good.
questions.why: The four habits are: see the world carefully, use evidence honestly, make wise choices, and serve the common good. Being the loudest is not one of them.

questions.text: Your family has $10 for groceries and wants three things. Which habit do you need most?
options: See the world carefully: read a map of the store.
Serve the common good: give the money away.
Use evidence honestly: check a source.
Make wise choices: think about the cost and the benefit.
questions.why: Making wise choices means thinking about costs and benefits before you spend. That is the habit Marketplace Hall trained.

questions.text: On the last day, the museum director said the museum was never really about the exhibits. What did she say the real exhibit was?
options: Each Exhibit Designer: you, and who you became.
The badges.
The building and its rooms.
The panels on the walls.
questions.why: The director said the rooms, panels, and badges were just the work. The real exhibit is each student: a young geographer-citizen.

questions.lesson: 3.11.03 Present the Evidence: Map, Source, and Virtue
questions.text: The word root aud means hear. What is an auditorium?
options: A room where you wash dishes.
A big tank for fish.
A big room with seats where people listen to a show or a talk.
A map of the world.
questions.why: Aud means hear, so an auditorium is a room where people listen. Audience, audio, and audible share the same root.
